paragraphs: Grushenka lived in the busiest part of town, close to the cathedral square. Her home was a small wooden lodge in the courtyard of the widow Morozov’s house, a big, old, very ugly stone building of two stories. The widow lived quietly with her two nieces, both unmarried and both getting on in years. She had no need to take a lodger. Yet everyone knew she had taken Grushenka in four years earlier for one reason only, to oblige her kinsman, the merchant Samsonov, who was known to be the girl’s protector. People said the jealous old man had parked his “favorite” with the widow Morozov so that the old woman would watch the new lodger’s conduct closely. That close watching soon turned out to be pointless. In the end the widow seldom saw Grushenka and never troubled her with supervision of any kind. True, it was four years since the old man had fetched her from the chief town of the province, a girl of eighteen, slim, delicate, shy, timid, dreamy and sad, and a good deal had happened since then. Little was known in town about her past, and what was known was vague. Nothing more had come out in the four years, even though many people had grown interested in the beautiful young woman that Agrafena Alexandrovna had turned into. Rumor had it that at seventeen she had been betrayed by someone, some officer, and dropped by him at once. The officer had gone off and later married, and Grushenka was left in poverty and disgrace. Yet it was also said that, although old Samsonov had pulled her out of destitution, she came of a respectable family from the clergy, and was the daughter of a deacon or some such person.

Now, four years later, the sensitive, wounded, pitiful little orphan had grown into a plump, rosy beauty of the true Russian kind, bold and strong-minded, proud and insolent. She had a head for business, was greedy for gain, thrifty and shrewd, and by fair means or foul had managed, so it was said, to build up a small fortune. On one point alone there was agreement. Grushenka was hard to get near. Apart from her aged protector, not a single man in those four years could boast of her favors. That was a plain fact, because plenty of men, especially in the last two years, had tried to win them. It had all been wasted effort. A few of these suitors had had to retreat in an undignified, even comical way, beaten by the firm and ironical resistance of this strong-willed young woman. People knew, too, that lately she had taken to what is called “speculation” and had shown a real talent for it. So many were saying she was no better than a Jew. She did not lend money at interest. But it was known, for example, that for some time she had been buying up bad debts for next to nothing, a tenth of their face value, in partnership with old Karamazov, and had then made ten times that value out of them.

The old widower Samsonov was a very rich man, and stingy and merciless. He bullied his grown sons. But in the last year, since falling ill and losing the use of his swollen legs, he had come greatly under the sway of his protégée. At first he had kept her strictly and in humble circumstances, “on Lenten fare,” as the wits of the time put it. But Grushenka had contrived to free herself, and at the same time she had planted in him an unlimited belief in her fidelity. The old man, long dead now, had once run a large business and was a remarkable character too, miserly and hard as flint. Her hold on him was so strong that he could not live without her (especially in the last two years). Even so, he settled no real fortune on her, and he would not have done it even if she had threatened to leave him. He did give her a small sum, though, and everyone was amazed when that came out.

“You’re a girl with brains,” he told her when he handed over eight thousand roubles, “so look out for yourself. But I’ll tell you this: besides your yearly allowance, which you get as before, you’ll have nothing more from me until the day I die, and I’ll leave you nothing in my will either.”

And he kept his word. He died and left everything to his sons, men he had treated as servants all his life, together with their wives and children. Grushenka was not even named in the will. All this was learned later. What he did give her was advice, on how to increase her capital, and he steered business her way.

Fyodor Pavlovitch first met Grushenka over a speculative deal, and to his own astonishment he ended up madly in love with her. Old Samsonov, sick as he was, found this enormously funny. It is worth noting that Grushenka was always completely and spontaneously frank with the old man. He seems to have been the one person in the world she was frank with. Lately, when Dmitri also entered the scene with his love, the old man stopped laughing. Instead, he once gave Grushenka some stern and serious advice.

“If you have to pick between them, father or son, pick the old man. Just make sure first that the old scoundrel will marry you and put some money in your name. But don’t go on with the captain. No good will come of that.”
Those were the actual words of the old rake, who could already feel that his death was near. He did in fact die five months afterwards.

I will mention in passing that many in our town knew about the grotesque, monstrous rivalry of the Karamazovs, father and son, over Grushenka. Yet hardly anyone understood what lay behind her attitude to the two of them. Even her two servants (after the catastrophe I will describe later) stated in court that she had received Dmitri Fyodorovitch only out of fear, because “he threatened to murder her.” These servants were an old cook, ailing and nearly deaf, who had come from Grushenka’s old home, and the cook’s granddaughter, a bright girl of twenty who worked as a maid. Grushenka lived very economically, and nothing around her was luxurious. The lodge had three rooms, furnished with mahogany pieces in the style of 1820, which belonged to her landlady.

By the time Rakitin and Alyosha went in it was quite dark, and yet no lamps had been lit. Grushenka lay in her drawing-room on the big, hard, clumsy sofa with its mahogany back, which was covered in worn, cracked leather. She had two white down pillows from her bed under her head and lay flat on her back, perfectly still, hands clasped behind her head. She was dressed as if she were expecting someone, in a black silk dress and a dainty lace fichu on her head that suited her well. A lace shawl lay over her shoulders, fastened with a heavy gold brooch. Someone was certainly expected. She lay there restless and tired, her face a little pale, her lips and eyes feverish, and her right foot kept tapping the arm of the sofa. The arrival of Rakitin and Alyosha set off a small commotion. From the hall they heard Grushenka jump up from the sofa and call out in a frightened voice, “Who’s there?” But the maid had met the visitors and answered her mistress at once.
“It’s not him, it’s nothing, just other visitors.”
“What’s going on?” muttered Rakitin, taking Alyosha into the drawing-room.

Grushenka stood by the sofa, still looking alarmed. A thick coil of dark brown hair had come loose from its lace covering and lay over her right shoulder. She did not notice, and did not tuck it back, until she had stared at the visitors and made out who they were.
“Oh, it’s you, Rakitin? You gave me such a fright. Who’s this you’ve brought? Who’s that with you? Good heavens, you’ve brought him!” she cried, recognizing Alyosha.
“Have someone bring candles!” said Rakitin, with the easy manner of a close friend who has the right to give orders in the house.

“Candles ... of course, candles.... Fenya, bring him a candle.... Well, you picked a fine moment to bring him!” she cried again, nodding at Alyosha. She turned to the mirror and began pinning up her hair with both hands, fast. She seemed put out.
“Haven’t I managed to please you?” asked Rakitin, almost offended on the spot.

“You scared me, Rakitin, that’s all.” Grushenka turned to Alyosha with a smile. “Don’t be afraid of me, my dear Alyosha. You can’t imagine how glad I am to see you, my unexpected guest. But you scared me, Rakitin. I thought it was Mitya bursting in. You see, I just tricked him. I made him promise to believe me, and I told him a lie. I said I was going to spend the evening with my old man, Kuzma Kuzmitch, and would be there late, counting his money. Every week I spend a whole evening with him, going through his accounts. We shut ourselves in, and he counts on the abacus while I sit and enter the figures in the book. I’m the only one he trusts. Mitya thinks I’m there, but I came back, and I’ve been sitting here locked in, waiting for news. How did Fenya come to let you in? Fenya, Fenya, run to the gate, open it and look about for the captain! Maybe he’s hiding and spying. I’m terribly afraid.”
“There’s nobody there, Agrafena Alexandrovna. I just looked out. I keep running to peek through the crack. I’m trembling with fear myself.”

“Are the shutters bolted, Fenya? And we have to close the curtains—that’s better!” She pulled the heavy curtains shut herself. “He’d burst in straight away if he saw a light. I’m afraid of your brother Mitya today, Alyosha.”
Grushenka was talking loudly, and for all her alarm she seemed very happy about something.
“Why are you so afraid of Mitya today?” asked Rakitin. “I’d have thought you weren’t shy of him. You wind him round your little finger.”

“I tell you, I’m waiting for news, priceless news, and so I don’t want Mitya at all. And I feel that he didn’t believe I’d stay at Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. He must be lying in ambush now, in the garden behind Fyodor Pavlovitch’s, watching for me. And if he’s there, he won’t come here, which is all the better! But I really did go to Kuzma Kuzmitch’s. Mitya took me there himself. I told him I’d stay till midnight, and I asked him to be sure to come at midnight and take me home. He left, and I sat ten minutes with Kuzma Kuzmitch and came back here. Ugh, I was scared. I ran, so as not to bump into him.”
“And why are you all dressed up? What a funny cap you’ve got on!”
“Aren’t you nosy, Rakitin! I tell you, I’m waiting for a message. If it comes, I’ll fly, I’ll gallop off, and you won’t see me again. That’s why I’m dressed up. To be ready.”
“And where are you flying to?”
“If you know too much, you’ll get old too soon.”
“Well, I never! You’re thrilled ... I’ve never seen you like this. You’re dressed up as if for a ball.” Rakitin looked her over from head to foot.
“Much you know about balls.”
“And you know a lot about them?”

“I’ve seen a ball. The year before last, Kuzma Kuzmitch’s son got married, and I watched from the gallery. Do you think I want to chat with you, Rakitin, with a prince like this standing here? What a guest! Alyosha, my dear boy, I look at you and can’t believe my eyes. Good heavens, did you really come to see me? To tell the truth, it never entered my head that I’d see you. I never thought you’d come to me. It’s not the right moment, but I’m awfully glad to see you all the same. Sit down on the sofa, here, there, my bright young moon. I still can’t take it in.... Ah, Rakitin, if only you’d brought him yesterday or the day before! But I’m glad as it is! Maybe it’s better that he came now, at a moment like this, and not the day before yesterday.”

She sat down on the sofa next to Alyosha, in high spirits, and looked at him with plain delight. And she truly was glad. She was not lying when she said so. Her eyes shone and her lips laughed, but it was a kindly, merry laugh. Alyosha had not expected such a kind look on her face.... Before yesterday he had hardly met her. He had formed a frightening idea of her, and yesterday he had been horribly upset by the spiteful, treacherous trick she had played on Katerina Ivanovna. Now he was greatly surprised to find her quite different from what he had expected. Crushed as he was by his own grief, he found his eyes resting on her with attention, almost without meaning to. Her whole manner seemed changed for the better since yesterday. In her speech there was hardly a trace of that sugary sweetness, and in her movements none of that sensuous softness. Everything about her was simple and good-natured. Her gestures were quick, direct and trusting. But she was very excited.
“Goodness, how everything comes together today!” she chattered on. “And why I’m so glad to see you, Alyosha, I couldn’t tell you myself! Ask me, and I couldn’t say.”
“Oh, come on, you don’t know why you’re glad?” said Rakitin, grinning. “You were always badgering me to bring him. You had some aim in mind, I suppose.”

“I had a different aim once, but that’s over, and this isn’t the time. Listen, I want you to have something nice. I’m in such a good mood. You sit down too, Rakitin. Why are you standing? You’ve sat down already? Rakitin never forgets to look after himself. Look, Alyosha, he’s sitting there across from us, so offended that I didn’t ask him to sit before you. Ugh, Rakitin, you’re such a one for taking offense!” laughed Grushenka. “Don’t be angry, Rakitin, I’m kind today. Why are you so gloomy, Alyosha? Are you afraid of me?” She peered into his eyes with merry mockery.
“He’s sad. The promotion hasn’t come through,” boomed Rakitin.
